title: Prometheus and Pandora
description: Prometheus steals fire; Pandora opens the jar of evils, keeping only Hope.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: In the beginning, the Titan Prometheus, whose name means Forethought, shaped men from earth and water, and taught them all the arts. But Zeus, king of the gods, kept fire from mortals. Prometheus stole fire, hiding a spark in a fennel stalk, and brought it to men. Zeus, in anger, chained Prometheus to a rock in the Caucasus, where an eagle tore his liver each day, and each night it healed — until Hercules freed him. To punish men, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to fashion Pandora, the first woman, beautiful and cunning, and each god gave her a gift. She was given to Epimetheus, Prometheus's brother, though Prometheus had warned him to accept nothing from Zeus. With her came a sealed jar. Curiosity overcame her; she opened it, and out flew all the evils — sickness, sorrow, toil, and strife — scattering over the world. She closed the lid just in time to keep Hope inside. And so men have evils, but also hope, to this day.

title: Deucalion's Flood
description: Deucalion and Pyrrha survive the flood and repeople the earth from stones.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: When men grew wicked, Zeus resolved to destroy them with a flood. But Deucalion, son of Prometheus, was just, and his wife Pyrrha was pious. Prometheus warned his son, who built an ark and stocked it. For nine days and nights the rain fell, and all the land was drowned. On the tenth day the ark rested on Mount Parnassus. Deucalion and Pyrrha stepped out, alone in the world. They prayed to the goddess Themis, who told them: 'Cast behind you the bones of your mother.' They understood: the earth is the mother of all; her bones are stones. They cast stones behind them, and the stones Deucalion threw became men, and those Pyrrha threw became women. And so the earth was peopled anew, a stonier, hardier race.

title: Apollo and Daphne
description: Daphne becomes a laurel tree to escape Apollo's love.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Apollo, proud after slaying the Python, mocked Cupid's bow. Cupid, in revenge, shot Apollo with a golden arrow of love, and Daphne, a river nymph, with a leaden arrow of aversion. Apollo pursued Daphne, who fled. As he gained, she cried to her father, the river god Peneus, to save her. Her feet rooted, bark covered her limbs, leaves crowned her head — she became a laurel tree. Apollo, grieving, embraced the tree, and declared the laurel evergreen and sacred to him; victors at his games should be crowned with it. And so the laurel honors Daphne still.

title: Perseus and Medusa
description: Perseus beheads Medusa with Athena's shield and saves Andromeda.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: King Acrisius, told by an oracle that his grandson would kill him, set his daughter Danae adrift in a chest. She bore Perseus, son of Zeus, who came to her as golden rain. They were saved, but the wicked King Polydectes, wanting Danae, sent Perseus to fetch the head of Medusa, whose gaze turned men to stone. The gods aided him: Athena gave a bright shield, Hermes winged sandals and a sickle sword, Hades a cap of invisibility. The Graeae, three sisters with one eye, told him where the nymphs kept these gifts, and where the Gorgons slept. Guided by Athena's reflection in his shield, Perseus struck off Medusa's sleeping head without looking at her. From her blood sprang Pegasus, the winged horse. On his way home, Perseus saw Andromeda chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster, for her mother had boasted. He slew the monster, married Andromeda, and with Medusa's head turned Polydectes and his court to stone. At games, a discus he threw struck and killed Acrisius, fulfilling the oracle. Perseus gave the head to Athena, who set it on her shield.

title: Theseus and the Minotaur
description: Theseus slays the Minotaur with Ariadne's thread but forgets the white sail.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Every nine years, Athens sent seven youths and seven maidens to Crete as tribute to the Minotaur, a monster half man, half bull, dwelling in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus. Theseus, son of King Aegeus, volunteered to go and slay the beast. At Crete, Ariadne, daughter of King Minos, fell in love with him and gave him a ball of thread to unwind as he entered the Labyrinth, so he could find his way back, and a sword. Theseus tied the thread at the door, found the Minotaur sleeping, slew it, and followed the thread out. He sailed home with Ariadne, but abandoned her on Naxos, where the god Dionysus wed her. Theseus, in his joy, forgot to hoist the white sail of success, keeping the black sail of mourning. Aegeus, watching from the cliffs, saw the black sail, believed his son dead, and cast himself into the sea, which is called the Aegean after him. Theseus became king of Athens.

title: The Twelve Labors of Hercules
description: Hercules atones through twelve impossible labors, from the Hydra to Cerberus.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Hercules, son of Zeus, in madness sent by Hera slew his wife and children. To atone, the oracle bade him serve King Eurystheus for twelve years. First, he slew the Nemean Lion, whose hide no weapon pierced, strangling it and wearing its skin. Second, the Lernaean Hydra, whose heads doubled when cut; with his nephew Iolaus cauterizing each neck, he slew it and dipped his arrows in its venom. Third, he captured the Ceryneian Hind alive after a year's chase. Fourth, the Erymanthian Boar, which he netted and carried alive. Fifth, he cleaned the Augean Stables, uncleaned for thirty years, by turning two rivers through them in a day. Sixth, he shot the Stymphalian Birds with his venom arrows, startling them with bronze rattles. Seventh, he captured the Cretan Bull alive and brought it to Greece. Eighth, the man-eating Mares of Diomedes, which he fed their master to, taming them. Ninth, the girdle of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, won after battle. Tenth, the cattle of the giant Geryon, slain with one venom arrow through three bodies. Eleventh, the golden Apples of the Hesperides, got by tricking Atlas into fetching them while Hercules held the sky. Twelfth, he descended to Hades and brought up Cerberus, the three-headed dog, alive, then returned him. Having done all, Hercules was free, and his fame is immortal.

title: Jason and the Golden Fleece
description: Jason wins the Golden Fleece with Medea's magic, then betrays her.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Jason, rightful heir of Iolcus, was sent by the usurper Pelias to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis, hoping he would die. Jason built the Argo and gathered heroes — Hercules, Orpheus, Castor and Pollux, and many more. After many adventures, they reached Colchis, where King Aeetes promised the Fleece if Jason yoked his fire-breathing bronze bulls, sowed dragon's teeth, and slew the armed men that sprang up. Medea, the king's sorceress daughter, fell in love with Jason and gave him magic ointment against fire and iron, and told him to throw a stone among the armed men so they would fight each other. Jason did all, but Aeetes broke his word. By night, Medea lulled the sleepless dragon guarding the Fleece, and Jason seized it. They fled, pursued; Medea killed her own brother and strewed his limbs in the sea to delay pursuit. They reached Iolcus, where Medea tricked Pelias's daughters into killing their father. But Jason later abandoned Medea for a new bride; in revenge, Medea slew his bride and her own children by Jason, and fled in a dragon chariot. Jason died, struck by a falling beam of the rotting Argo.

title: The Trojan War
description: A golden apple's judgment leads to ten years of war and Troy's fall.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: At the wedding of Peleus, Eris, goddess of discord, threw a golden apple marked 'To the fairest.' Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite quarreled; Zeus bade Paris, prince of Troy, judge. Each offered bribes: Hera, power; Athena, wisdom and victory; Aphrodite, the most beautiful woman in the world — Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta. Paris chose Aphrodite. He went to Sparta and carried Helen to Troy. Menelaus and his brother Agamemnon summoned all Greece; a thousand ships sailed. For ten years they besieged Troy. Achilles, greatest of the Greeks, quarreled with Agamemnon and withdrew, till his friend Patroclus was slain by Hector, prince of Troy. Achilles returned, slew Hector, and dragged his body round the walls. Paris slew Achilles with an arrow in his heel, his one vulnerable spot. At last Odysseus devised the Wooden Horse: the Greeks pretended to sail away, leaving a great horse as an offering. The Trojans dragged it in. At night, Greeks hidden inside opened the gates; Troy was sacked and burned. Helen was restored to Menelaus. The heroes' returns were long and cruel — none crueler than Odysseus's ten years of wandering.

title: Odysseus and the Cyclops
description: 'Nobody' blinds the Cyclops Polyphemus and escapes beneath the rams.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Sailing home from Troy, Odysseus and his men landed on the island of the Cyclopes, one-eyed giants. They entered the cave of Polyphemus, who rolled a great stone across the mouth and, finding them, ate two for supper and two for breakfast. Odysseus gave him strong wine, and when Polyphemus asked his name, Odysseus said 'Nobody.' Drunk, the giant slept. Odysseus heated a great stake and, with his men, drove it into the Cyclops's single eye, blinding him. In the morning, Polyphemus let his sheep out, feeling each back, but Odysseus and his men clung beneath the rams' bellies and escaped. From the ship, Odysseus taunted him, revealing his true name. Polyphemus prayed to his father Poseidon for vengeance, and Poseidon hounded Odysseus for ten years. So pride after cunning cost Odysseus dear.

title: Orpheus and Eurydice
description: Orpheus loses Eurydice twice by looking back at the threshold.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Orpheus, greatest of musicians, loved Eurydice. On their wedding day, she was bitten by a serpent and died. Orpheus descended to Hades, charming Charon, Cerberus, and the very ghosts with his lyre. Hades and Persephone, moved, allowed Eurydice to follow him to the upper world, on one condition: he must not look back till they reached the light. Orpheus led her up the dark path, and, just at the threshold, doubting, he looked back — and she was gone, forever. Wild with grief, he shunned all women; the Maenads, in frenzy, tore him apart. His head, cast into the Hebrus, floated still singing to Lesbos. And in the underworld, Orpheus and Eurydice walk together at last, he never now needing to look back.

title: King Midas
description: Midas's golden touch starves him; later he grows ass's ears.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Silenus, companion of Dionysus, wandered drunk into the rose gardens of King Midas, who entertained him kindly for ten days and returned him to the god. Dionysus offered Midas any wish. Midas wished that all he touched might turn to gold. At first he rejoiced: stones, branches, all gold. But his food turned to gold in his mouth, his drink, and when he embraced his daughter, she became a golden statue. Starving amid gold, Midas begged release. Dionysus bade him wash in the river Pactolus, which carried the curse away — its sands are golden to this day. Later, Midas judged a music contest between Apollo and Pan, and, preferring Pan's pipes, Apollo gave him ass's ears. Midas hid them under a cap, but his barber, bursting to tell, whispered it into a hole in the ground. Reeds grew there, and whispered to the wind: 'King Midas has ass's ears.' And so all the world knew.

title: Daedalus and Icarus
description: Icarus flies too near the sun and falls; Daedalus mourns.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Daedalus, greatest of craftsmen, built the Labyrinth for King Minos of Crete. When he helped Theseus escape it, Minos imprisoned Daedalus and his son Icarus in a tower. Daedalus fashioned wings of feathers and wax. 'Fly the middle course,' he warned Icarus; 'neither too low, lest the sea damp the wings, nor too high, lest the sun melt the wax.' They leapt from the tower and flew. Icarus, exulting, soared higher and higher, till the sun melted the wax; the feathers scattered, and he fell into the sea that bears his name, the Icarian. Daedalus flew on, grieving, to Sicily, where King Cocalus sheltered him. Minos pursued, but Cocalus's daughters scalded Minos to death in his bath. Daedalus lived honored, but never ceased to mourn his son.

title: Persephone and Hades
description: Six pomegranate seeds divide Persephone between two worlds, making the seasons.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Persephone, daughter of Demeter, goddess of harvest, was gathering flowers when the earth opened and Hades, lord of the underworld, carried her off to be his queen. Demeter searched the world, and in grief let the crops wither; men starved. Zeus, pressed by famine, sent Hermes to bring Persephone back. But she had eaten six pomegranate seeds in the underworld, and none who eat there may wholly return. So it was decreed: Persephone spends six months with Hades, and six with her mother. When she is below, Demeter mourns, and it is winter; when she returns, the earth blooms, and it is spring. And so the seasons turn.

title: Narcissus and Echo
description: Narcissus loves his own reflection; Echo fades to a voice.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Echo was a nymph who loved to talk, and Hera, to punish her chatter, took her voice, leaving only the power to repeat the last words spoken to her. Echo loved the beautiful youth Narcissus, but he scorned her, as he scorned all lovers. Pining, she faded till only her voice remained among the rocks. Nemesis, to punish Narcissus's cruelty, led him to a still pool. Seeing his own reflection, he fell in love with it, not knowing it was himself. He pined away at the pool's edge, and where he died sprang the flower that bears his name, the narcissus. And Echo still answers in lonely places.

title: Arachne
description: Arachne outweaves Athena and is turned into a spider.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Arachne was a Lydian maiden whose weaving was so fine that the nymphs came to watch. Proud, she boasted she wove better than Athena herself. Athena, disguised as an old woman, warned her, but Arachne challenged the goddess to a contest. Athena wove the gods in glory; Arachne wove the gods' misdeeds — their deceptions and cruelties — so skillfully that even Athena could find no fault, but was enraged at the insult. She tore Arachne's web and struck her with her shuttle. Arachne, in shame, hanged herself; Athena, pitying, loosened the rope and turned her into a spider, to weave forever. And spiders descend from Arachne.

title: Pygmalion
description: A sculptor's ivory maiden comes to life through Aphrodite's pity.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Pygmalion was a sculptor of Cyprus who despised women, and carved from ivory a maiden so beautiful that he fell in love with his own work. He dressed the statue, brought it gifts, and prayed to Aphrodite to give him a wife like his ivory maid. On Aphrodite's festival day, he prayed again, and the goddess, pitying him, breathed life into the ivory. The statue warmed, blushed, and lived. Pygmalion married her, and they had a son, Paphos. And Aphrodite blessed their union.

title: Bellerophon and Pegasus
description: Bellerophon tames Pegasus, slays the Chimaera, then falls through pride.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Bellerophon, exiled for a crime he did not commit, came to King Proetus, whose wife falsely accused him. Proetus sent him to King Iobates with a sealed letter bidding his death. Iobates, unwilling to slay a guest, set him impossible tasks: first, to kill the Chimaera, a monster of lion, goat, and serpent that breathed fire. Bellerophon, by Athena's counsel, tamed Pegasus, the winged horse sprung from Medusa's blood, with a golden bridle. Mounted, he slew the Chimaera with arrows and a lead-tipped spear that melted in its throat. Then he defeated the Amazons and the Solymi. Iobates, seeing the gods favored him, gave him his daughter and half his kingdom. But pride seized Bellerophon; he tried to fly Pegasus to Olympus. Zeus sent a gadfly that stung Pegasus, who threw his rider. Bellerophon fell, blinded and lame, and wandered lonely till he died. Pegasus flies still among the stars.

title: Oedipus
description: Oedipus fulfills the oracle he fled: he kills his father, weds his mother.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Laius, king of Thebes, was told by an oracle that his son would kill him. When Oedipus was born, Laius pierced his ankles and left him on a mountain. A shepherd saved him, and he was raised by the king of Corinth as his son. Grown, Oedipus heard the oracle and, believing Corinth's king his father, fled. At a crossroads, he quarreled with an old man over the way and killed him — it was Laius. At Thebes, the Sphinx asked: 'What walks on four feet in the morning, two at noon, three in the evening?' Oedipus answered: 'Man.' The Sphinx cast herself down, and Thebes made Oedipus king, giving him Laius's widow Jocasta to wife. They had four children. Then plague struck Thebes; the oracle said the killer of Laius must be found. Oedipus cursed the killer — and learned, step by step, that he himself was the killer, the son of Laius, the husband of his mother. Jocasta hanged herself; Oedipus blinded himself with her brooches, and wandered, led by his daughter Antigone, till the gods granted him a mysterious, honored death at Colonus.

title: Atalanta
description: Atalanta loses a footrace to three golden apples and marries the winner.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Atalanta was left on a mountain as a babe and suckled by a she-bear; she grew into the swiftest huntress in Greece, and sailed with the Argonauts, and was first to wound the Calydonian Boar. Many sought her hand; she declared she would marry only the man who outran her, and the losers should die. Many died. Then came Hippomenes, who prayed to Aphrodite. The goddess gave him three golden apples. In the race, when Atalanta gained, he dropped an apple; she stooped to pick it up, losing ground. Thrice he did this, and won by a step. They married happily. But Hippomenes forgot to thank Aphrodite, and she turned them both into lions for profaning her shrine. And lions they remain.

title: Cupid and Psyche
description: Psyche's forbidden look costs her Cupid; her trials win him back.
author: Traditional (Greek myth)

chapters.title: Complete Text
chapters.text: Psyche was so beautiful that men worshipped her instead of Venus. The jealous goddess bade her son Cupid make Psyche love a monster, but Cupid himself fell in love with her. He carried her to a splendid palace, where she lived in luxury, visited each night by a husband she might never see. Her jealous sisters persuaded her to look; she lit a lamp, saw the beautiful god, and a drop of hot oil woke him. He fled, and the palace vanished. Psyche wandered, seeking him, and came at last to Venus, who set her cruel tasks: sorting a mountain of grain (ants helped), fetching golden wool (reeds advised her), drawing water from the Styx (an eagle helped), and bringing beauty from Proserpine in a box — which she must not open. Curiosity won; she opened it and fell into a deathly sleep. Cupid, forgiving, woke her, and Jupiter made her immortal. Venus was appeased, and Cupid and Psyche were wed among the gods.
